4:["$","$L2","1",{"href":"/areas/civil-rights","className":"text-[9px] uppercase tracking-tighter bg-sand px-2 py-1 border border-gold/20 hover:border-gold transition-colors","children":"Civil Rights"}]
9:T426,Cornelia Rosina "Cutchie" Jones (September 10, 1907 – December 23, 1979) occupies a towering, trailblazing place in the political and social history of the Dutch Caribbean. Universally celebrated and affectionately remembered across the island as "Ma Jones" or "Cutchie," she shattered centuries of gender barriers by becoming the first woman to serve on the Island Council of Saba in August 1953. This historic achievement simultaneously earned her the distinction of being the first female public officeholder in the entire Dutch Windward Islands—comprising Saba, Sint Eustatius, and Sint Maarten. Operating during an era when formal political power was exclusively dominated by men, Jones emerged as a forceful, compassionate leader who bridged socio-economic and racial divides. Alongside her legislative milestones, she served for decades as the celebrated manager of the Government Guesthouse, acting as the island's premier diplomat, culinary ambassador, and cultural hostess to visiting royalty, international statesmen, and regional leaders such as tranquil, elevated village of St. John's on the island of Saba. Her birth occurred during a remarkable period of demographic and social transformation in the Dutch Caribbean. She was born to Mary Jane Hassell, a white Saban woman from one of the island's oldest European settlement families, and Fernandus Jones, a skilled Black Saban sailor and mariner. Growing up in a household representing the rich, interwoven racial heritage of Saba, young Cornelia developed an extraordinary resilience and a deep understanding of the island's diverse social fabric."}],"\n","$Lb","\n","$Lc","\n","$Ld","\n","$Le","\n","$Lf","\n","$L10","\n","$L11","\n","$L12","\n","$L13","\n","$L14","\n","$L15","\n","$L16","\n","$L17","\n","$L18","\n","$L19","\n","$L1a","\n","$L1b","\n","$L1c","\n","$L1d","\n","$L1e","\n","$L1f","\n","$L20"]}]]}],"$L21","$L22",false]}],"$L23"]}]

b:["$","p","p-3",{"children":"During the early twentieth century, Saba's economy was driven by maritime trade. A vast majority of the island's working-age men were employed on foreign merchant vessels, naval ships, and whaling expeditions, often away from home for months or years at a time. Consequently, Saba functioned as a unique matriarchal society in daily practice. Women managed household economies, cultivated hillside subsistence crops, maintained community schools, and produced exquisite drawn-thread lacework (\"Saba Lace\") that was exported globally. Growing up surrounded by fiercely independent, capable women, Jones internalized early on that female leadership was the true backbone of island survival, even if formal political governance remained barred to them."}]
c:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"A community is built not merely by the laws enacted in council chambers, but by the warmth, sustenance, and dignity we extend to one another under our own roofs.\""}],"\n"]}]
d:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":"The Government Guesthouse: Hostess to the World"}]
e:["$","p","p-4",{"children":"Before entering formal political life, Cornelia Jones established her reputation as the most hospitable and formidable presence on Saba through her leadership of the official Government Guesthouse. In an era long before modern hotels, commercial resorts, or regular aviation connected Saba to the outside world, the Government Guesthouse—situated first in the administrative capital of The Bottom and later expanded to Windwardside—served as the sole diplomatic, administrative, and social hub of the island."}]
f:["$","p","p-5",{"children":"As the manager, head hostess, and master chef of the Government Guesthouse, \"Cutchie\" Jones held a position of profound informal influence. The guesthouse hosted Dutch colonial governors, visiting ministers from The Hague, Caribbean parliamentarians, international journalists, scientific researchers, and esteemed travel writers. Jones ran the establishment with impeccable standards, warmth, and commanding authority. Conversations at her dining table shaped island policy and regional perceptions. Her culinary mastery—blending traditional Saban flavors with European refinement—became legendary across the West Indies. Visiting leaders quickly learned that to understand the true pulse, needs, and grievances of the Saban people, one first had to listen to the wise counsel of Ma Jones over dinner."}]
10:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"Political Awakening and Universal Suffrage"}]
11:["$","p","p-6",{"children":["The aftermath of World War II catalyzed a massive political awakening across the Dutch Caribbean. In 1948, universal adult suffrage was officially enacted throughout the Netherlands Antilles, granting women the legal right to vote and stand for public office for the first time. As political movements organized across the islands under pioneers like ",["$","$La","a-0",{"slug":"efrain-jonckheer","href":"/profiles/efrain-jonckheer","children":"Efraín Jonckheer"}]," in Curaçao, Saban women began asserting their voice in municipal affairs."]}]
12:["$","p","p-7",{"children":["Recognizing that true community advancement required direct legislative participation, Jones formally entered the political arena in 1951. She aligned herself with the ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Nationale Volkspartij"}]," (NVP / National People's Party), a dynamic political organization dedicated to social welfare, local infrastructure improvement, and expanded political representation for the working classes. Her reputation for integrity, benevolence, and administrative competence made her an immediately formidable candidate on the NVP ticket."]}]
13:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"Shattering the Glass Ceiling: The Historic Appointment of 1953"}]
14:["$","p","p-8",{"children":"The defining moment of Jones's political career—and a watershed event in Caribbean gender equality—arrived in August 1953. Following the resignation of Island Council member Kenneth Peterson, Cornelia Rosina Jones was officially called to take her seat on the Island Council of Saba. When she walked into the historic council chambers in The Bottom and took her oath of office, she completely shattered a centuries-old male monopoly on political power."}]
15:["$","p","p-9",{"children":"Her accession made her the very first woman to serve on the Saba Island Council and the first female public officeholder in the history of the Dutch Windward Islands. In a political culture where debates had long been conducted exclusively by male merchants and landowners, Jones brought a refreshing, pragmatic, and deeply human-centric perspective to municipal governance."}]
16:["$","p","p-10",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5a/Flag_of_Saba.svg","alt":"Flag of Saba"}]}]
17:["$","h3","h3-5",{"children":"Legislative Priorities and Community Leadership"}]
18:["$","p","p-11",{"children":"During her tenure on the Island Council, Jones proved to be a pragmatic and collaborative lawmaker who prioritized the practical welfare of ordinary Sabans above partisan squabbling. She utilized her legislative platform to champion critical social infrastructure that directly impacted daily life. Among her top priorities were the expansion of public health initiatives, the improvement of clean sanitation and cistern water catchment systems, support for primary education, and better working conditions for civil servants and laborers."}]
19:["$","p","p-12",{"children":["Jones understood that Saba's geographical isolation required robust government support for vulnerable populations, particularly the elderly and single mothers whose husbands were lost at sea or working abroad. Her legislative advocacy worked in seamless tandem with her role at the Government Guesthouse; she frequently used her direct personal access to visiting federal dignitaries from Curaçao and the Netherlands—including future leaders like ",["$","$La","a-0",{"slug":"juancho-evertsz","href":"/profiles/juancho-evertsz","children":"Juancho Evertsz"}],"—to lobby effectively for increased federal subsidies and infrastructural grants for Saba."]}]
1a:["$","blockquote","blockquote-1",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"When a woman steps into the halls of governance, she carries with her the hopes of every child and the struggles of every family. Our duty is to ensure that power serves the vulnerable, not just the privileged.\""}],"\n"]}]
1b:["$","h3","h3-6",{"children":"Royal Honor and Later Years"}]
1c:["$","p","p-13",{"children":"Cornelia Jones's extraordinary dual career of public service and diplomatic hospitality did not go unnoticed by the Crown. In solemn recognition of her tireless devotion to the community, her pioneering role in Caribbean women's political leadership, and her exemplary service as the hostess of Saba, Queen Juliana of the Netherlands bestowed upon her a prestigious Royal Decoration. This knighthood cemented her status as one of the most respected citizens in the Kingdom of the Netherlands."}]
1d:["$","p","p-14",{"children":"Even after stepping down from active electoral politics, Ma Jones remained the revered matriarch of Saban society. Her home in The Bottom continued to function as an informal community center where politicians, citizens, and youth sought advice, mediation, and encouragement. She remained a steadfast voice for civic unity and cultural preservation until her peaceful passing on December 23, 1979, at the age of 72."}]
1e:["$","h3","h3-7",{"children":"Enduring Legacy and Modern Impact"}]
1f:["$","p","p-15",{"children":["The historical legacy of Cornelia Rosina \"Cutchie\" Jones continues to resonate powerfully across the Caribbean today. By courageously taking her seat on the Island Council in 1953, she blazed a trail that made it possible for subsequent generations of female leaders—such as future Saban commissioners, island councilors, and Prime Minister ",["$","$La","a-0",{"slug":"maria-liberia-peters","href":"/profiles/maria-liberia-peters","children":"Maria Liberia-Peters"}],"—to rise to the highest levels of governance without questioning their rightful place in the corridors of power."]}]
20:["$","p","p-16",{"children":"In contemporary Saba, her memory is cherished as a symbol of unity, hospitality, and female empowerment. To ensure that her monumental contributions are permanently permanently etched into the consciousness of future generations, one of the primary academic buildings at the Saba Comprehensive School was formally named in her honor. Today, students walking through the Cornelia Jones house are reminded daily of the pioneering Saban woman of mixed heritage who governed with grace, fed the world with warmth, and led her island into a more equitable democratic future."}]
21:["$","$L27",null,{"title":"Learn about the legacy of Cornelia Jones","url":"https://caribbeanlegacyarchive.com/profiles/cornelia-jones"}]
28:T6d4,Cornelia Rosina "Cutchie" Jones made historic, groundbreaking contributions to the political and cultural development of the Caribbean by becoming the first woman to serve on the Island Council of Saba in August 1953, which simultaneously made her the first female public officeholder in the entire Dutch Windward Islands. Shattering centuries of male political dominance, she utilized her legislative platform within the National People's Party (NVP) to champion essential socio-economic reforms, public healthcare improvements, educational advancements, and infrastructural development for the working-class and vulnerable populations of Saba. Her courageous entry into public office blazed a permanent trail for gender equality in Caribbean governance, laying the groundwork for future generations of female parliamentarians, commissioners, and regional leaders across the Netherlands Antilles.

Equally significant was her cultural and diplomatic contribution as the long-serving manager and consummate hostess of the official Government Guesthouse in Saba. In an era before modern tourism, Jones acted as the island's primary diplomatic and social ambassador, hosting colonial governors, royal emissaries, international journalists, and Caribbean statespersons with legendary hospitality and culinary brilliance. Through her wise informal counsel and direct advocacy with visiting dignitaries, she successfully lobbied for crucial federal investments in Saban infrastructure. Honored with a Royal Decoration by Queen Juliana of the Netherlands and commemorated with a campus building named in her honor at the Saba Comprehensive School, Cornelia Jones remains an immortal pillar of Saban heritage, matriarchal leadership, and civic dedication.22:["$","div",null,{"className":"mb-12 pt-12 border-t border-gold/10","children":[["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Major Contributions"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed bg-white p-8 border-l-4 border-tropical-green shadow-sm","children":"$28"}]]}]
